examples of it and report back." I guess this is it now.

find

So here is a short article of what is a "Flag Limit" since it is widely used

14517

lately. It should help avoid confusion. As Ifmyante said a while back: "If there's an area of indecision, it manifests itself as a flag. The limits of this flag then become the new zones." He also said that "the Flag Limit represents the end of the momentum". All credit goes to him, for bringing it to my attention.

Below are some graphic representations to simplify things before we go on real examples.

and some real examples follow

Some of course are more messy than others, the trick here is to take the best shaped and clear ones. The whole Flag area has a lot more plays than the FTB alone. Its your job, if you like, to take this basic setup and expand on it. I don’t list any other plays here because it will only confuse you for now and miss the basic point. Discussion will continue in your blogs, if you have questions post in the school room. Best of luck to everyone.

by Harry

some are cleaner than others. just work with what you have each time. ok, for flag limits two things are important.

as IF said "they signify the end of the momentum" and also we look for them at previous important areas, like obvious SR for example. why? because after the pole, price tries to get back into the area and fails, making a decision and this is our flag limit. so on first return of the price, since the decision has already been made, we can expect a reaction. also, the flag limit area may hold for more tries than the first visit and is valid till broken (but i dont advise anyone to trade it a 2nd time)

after the flag limit is engulfed price is free to travel back to the base of the pole, like in Hotochin's example.

Hi all! I have a question about flag, flag limits and flags, the question is about it's anatomy exactly.

I wonder whether my thoughts are correct. To me flags (I mean flag limit + indecision area - flag, without a pole) looks like that they are places where pro money are doing one of the two things: - distribute orders: in this situation we have a flag which means trend reversal - accumulate orders: in this situation we have a flag which means trend continuation

The basis of my thoughts is that: when we have a large pole (pro money is buying/selling, let's exclude cases where pole's reason is low liquidity). There must be a place where these accumulated positions will be distributed. To me such places are flags. It must take time to distribute so much positions, because if big boys would do it in one shot, we would have a pole in opposite direction (it is not good idea).

Are my thoughts correct, or I misunderstand something?

Thanks! Chris

Harry

Something Wulfgar and Harry pointed out,

1. When ever a S/D zone is broken or consumed, it becomes the opposite, the strength of which is determined by the speed at which the zone was broken. 1. Well respected SR flip, 2. Broken by a momentum candle in a LTF (M5, M15) so that Institutions did not have time to enter their positions. 3. Price takes a bit of time to filter back to the D turned S or vice versa.

Hi Hoto,

For me a broken FL is just Broke... If I understand the FTR concept correctly, after price engulfs something important like a FL, it tries to return to origin of the drop/rally and fails. I may not have the best definition of FTR, but for me, if that area that failed does not print a new low/high then it is no FTR and I will steer away from it. Also an FTR can relate to any other important area, be it SR, SD, Swap, another FTR or even a FL. But... IMHO an FTR to a FL has to happen before that FL breaks. FTR should highlight bullish/bearish strength, so it has to happen before the opponent takes control.

Now as far as my diagram above is concerned, I was just trying to highlight the relationship of price (after a break of FL) to the limits of that same FL once price retraces back into it in the future. you read my mind Harry. My goal was to spike some interest in this discussion on FL's and not only draw lines at SR's and boxes around FL.

Here are some comments.

Where to enter in a FLAG? Look for a decision within its limits where price broke the extreme. Sometimes this is easy to spot moving lower in TFs. Look for fresh S/D within the FL zone.

What happens when a FL is engulfed? Engulfed FL is a good sign Price wants to fill the base of the FL pole. This is something I like to use as criteria for an FTR trade setup.

Why do some FTB trades at FL's work and others don't? A FLAG should break a key level/area to be considered significant. When a bases pole has momentum coming out of a significant price level, SD Zone, SR Flip, etc, and the FL engulfs a key level/area (SR, SD, FL), this is criteria that is important when considering entering on RT to the FL area.

@piphop As I understand it a FL is a decision point that confines a larger flag/range/rectangle. Depending on the time frame, the larger flag represents accumulation or distribution by larger entities (or just fluctuation in a range on HTFs), which by its very nature means a pause in the "trend," so the momentum of a larger movement is, at that point, considered lost (as you saw, price changed direction, though it is common for momentum to pick up in the same direction again) Also, I understand that what distinguishes a RBR/DBR/etc. from a FL is price's tendency to form a flag adjacent to that level so the term FL cant really be used until a FTB. Flags happen when price pulls over on the side of the road to look at its map. p=m*v where v=0, if you will As always, if I'm wrong, someone please correct me for pophop's sake.

Yes, but in this case those spikes are Fake Outs, with the FO they (ITs) make retail traders to buy, so they will have people to sell. Remember, to buy you need to have a seller, and to sell you need someone to buy.

So they pull the price a little bit higher to the other flag that I show you, to:

1. take the pending orders in the flag. 2. take the stop loss of the traders that went short. 3. take the SL of the traders that trade the breakout.

By this FO they found the liquidity to heavily sell, it’s a trap.

That’s why I tell you to remember your quote, price didn’t respect the FL, because there were the ITs pulling the price a little bit higher to start selling. Some say this is manipulation, but I think that manipulation is part of the Price Action and Order Flow, in the end they are the ones that move the market, not us.

akifusenet,

You're asking some very good questions which I was asking myself a month or so ago!! I don't have all the solutions but hopefully what I've learned is of some help. First, about the significance of flag limits...some of them are more "localized" flag limits. For example, FL1 is an engulf of a local high, while FL2 is more of an engulf of the flag area to the left (where we see price meandering around without any new poles). To me that tells me FL2 is probably the more significant than FL1 since we're engulfing a larger zone. FL3 is another story of price engulfing a smaller flag area, but it did work nicely several times as you see.

Now onto the more difficult question which I've been searching for as well...FL2 - was it engulfed or not? I don't think so. First, I'm not entirely sure that FL2 is the actual flag limit or not. On the M1 chart where you can't zoom much farther unless you have a tick chart, it's possible that the actual FL extends closer to the "SR" area. If it doesn't and price did move below it, I still see this as an FTR which would show up on higher time frames as a FL in its own right (they are the same thing). Note how price broke above the S/R, tried to get back in, and then moved above the original breakout high, confirming an FTR. Where would I place the stop? Well, I wouldn't have been completely comfortable with that original FL2 zone for previously mentioned reasons, but if I were, I would have placed it a pip or so below the base of it given this is an M1 chart. If I were stopped out, I would have probably given the FTR a try as well since it's valid too. Others might put it beyond the S/R but that isn't something I care to do. Note how in your bottom center graphic that FL2 may have been exceeded by a pip or so but if you use the FTR area it would have stayed within bounds.

Significance of FL/FTR has nothing to do with time but with what kind of flag area was engulfed. Are we looking at a strong engulf of a huge daily flag area or are we looking at price engulfing a local flag on the M1? That's what makes the difference in my experience.

Keep in mind this is just my two cents, but I hope it helps. This is an area of interest for me as well.

Hi John,

this question is bothering many of us, including me. The problem is, we are looking for perfection, for something what works 100% of the time. I think, one is only wasting the time doing it. How many weeks, months, years are we wasting looking for answers in forums with clear rules wich work 100% of the time? This is a process oriented approach and you have some very good rules here which you have to build on. But to do, you have to do your own research. There is no way around it. No short cuts. If you take one rule from marketpedia and and go over charts and use the rule in a consistent manner (you use this rule the same way every time), you will get results in terms of if it works or not, in which circumstances etc. You then come to the conclusion, how to trade it. If it for example doesn't work 80% of the time, that's perfect, because you know that when you do the opposite, it will work What I am trying to say is, stop wasting the time searching for perfection and start working on your own unique style, which will work for you and which you will understand because you have built it from the scratch. The process counts.

The other thing which is stopping us from improving is the endless searching for 100% accuracy, when there simply is no need for 100% accuracy. We have to accept that we won't be right every time and that is fine because we can still make money.

Take something what you think you understand or what you like and do as detailed research on it as you can, then build on it. That's really it:)

Whilst it is true that a FL is formed after the break of any high or low, it does not necessarily make it an important FL. The important ones are the ones that form after the break of important opposing levels

In your chart - what is the significance of the green box? What important opposing level was broken that led to its formation? I see you've drawn on a small box that it broke - presumably off something on M1 - but do you think that the break of a small M1 level is as important as the break of the highs to the left, at which price spent a long time? Not trying to be patronising, forgive me if it comes off that way, but just trying to get you to think about it. "Look left, and then look left again" is a great IF quote.

Here's the AU move as I see it:

1075

Remember, spotting important levels is only half of the battle. Reading the movement of price as well is what gives us the context on which to base decisions. Just a zone by itself is only half of the equation.

Try not to get too hung up on "needing" to always find exact single tiny FLs on M1. You will drive yourself mad. Instead, find the big obvious ones on higher timeframes, draw a box around the whole FL, and try to focus on just reading the movement of price as it approaches, and look for any surges that give us a clue to when the big boys have entered the market.

How did it approach the zone? Did it surge into it? Did it CP? What was the direction of the last large surge in price, bullish or bearish? Have we reached the best level to turn price from, and therefore can we expect a FO? Have we reached the base of the move yet? Is the FL we are looking at inside daily supply/demand? H4? Weekly?

Remember the RTM method is pieces of a jigsaw which all must be pieced together to make full sense of price movement. Focusing exclusively on just one part will cause you to miss the bigger picture. Quite often if we are patient, price will tell us what it wants to do, and we can just get along for the ride.

FLs are not exactly FTRs. FL's contain FTRs. FL's ecompass the whole range of hesitation after engulf. FTR's are decision points within FL to continue.

FTR's are decision points that happen either before or after engulf. So, for FLs we are interested in DP to continue after engulf.

Naturally, when there is an engulf, we can find an FTR (a DP to engulf), and then we can find a FL, that contains a DP to continue (which is also an FTR, but we say it's an FL to point out the difference). Sometimes we can't find an FL, because we have a fakeout and price reverses.
